content: Atrial fibrillation, commonly referred to as AFib or AF, is the most frequently treated type of heart arrhythmia. An arrhythmia occurs when the heart beats too slowly, too quickly, or in an irregular pattern. In AFib, the normal rhythmic contractions of the upper chambers of the heart (the atria) become irregular, which disrupts the efficient flow of blood from the atria to the lower chambers (the ventricles). This condition can manifest as brief episodes or persist as a chronic, permanent issue. AFib is a significant public health concern. It is projected that approximately 12.1 million individuals in the United States will have AFib by 2030. In 2021, AFib was documented on 232,030 death certificates, with 28,037 of those cases listing it as the primary cause of death. People of European ancestry are statistically more likely to develop AFib compared to Black individuals. Additionally, since the prevalence of AFib increases with age and women generally live longer than men, more women are affected by this condition than men. Some individuals with AFib may remain asymptomatic and unaware of their condition. However, others may experience symptoms such as an irregular heartbeat, heart palpitations (described as rapid, fluttering, or pounding sensations), lightheadedness, extreme fatigue, shortness of breath, or chest pain. The likelihood of developing AFib increases with advancing age. High blood pressure, which also becomes more common with age, is responsible for approximately 20% of AFib cases. Other risk factors include obesity, European ancestry, diabetes, heart failure, ischemic heart disease, hyperthyroidism, chronic kidney disease, moderate to heavy alcohol consumption, smoking, and enlargement of the left-sided heart chambers. AFib is closely linked to an elevated risk of stroke. When other standard stroke risk factors are accounted for, AFib is associated with a fivefold increase in the risk of ischemic stroke. Approximately one in seven strokes is caused by complications related to AFib. Strokes resulting from AFib tend to be more severe compared to those caused by other underlying conditions. Strokes occur when blood flow to the brain is obstructed, either by a blood clot or by fatty deposits (plaque) within the blood vessel walls. Treatment for AFib typically involves a combination of approaches. Medications may be prescribed to regulate the heart's rhythm and rate. Blood-thinning medications are often used to prevent the formation of blood clots and to reduce the risk of stroke. In some cases, surgical interventions may be necessary. Additionally, managing risk factors through lifestyle modifications and medications is an essential component of treatment. AFib has significant consequences for public health. Each year in the United States, there are over 454,000 hospitalizations where AFib is the primary diagnosis. The condition contributes to approximately 158,000 deaths annually. Over the past two decades, the mortality rate associated with AFib, whether as a primary or contributing cause, has been steadily increasing. Geographically, counties with the highest rates of hospitalizations due to cardiac dysrhythmias, including AFib, are predominantly located in states such as Florida, Georgia, Alabama, Arkansas, Kentucky, North Carolina, West Virginia, Ohio, and Michigan. Additional clusters of high hospitalization rates are observed in parts of Texas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Missouri, Illinois, Tennessee, South Carolina, Indiana, Virginia, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, New York, Vermont, and Maine.
